data.title: Competitive Balance in Professional League of Legends
data.research_question: How unequal are regular-season results within leagues, and has balance changed over time?
data.motivation: The uncertainty-of-outcome hypothesis in sports economics links fan interest to balanced competition. Esports leagues differ in format (franchised vs promotion and relegation), which makes balance worth measuring rather than assuming.
methodology: Unit of analysis: one league split (league + season + split), regular-season games only; international events and playoffs excluded; teams with fewer than 5 games left out.
Share variable: each team's share of all regular-season wins in the split (not prize money, which the source does not contain).
Noll-Scully ratio: sd of team win% divided by the sd expected if every game were a coin flip (0.5/sqrt(games per team)). 1 = as balanced as chance; higher = less balanced.
HHI of win shares (normalised: 0 = equal shares, 1 = one team has every win), Gini coefficient of wins and Lorenz curves of wins per split.
Title side: regular-season rank of each derived champion.
Upset rate: share of games won by the lower pre-game Elo team, by quarter.
limitations: Short splits make Noll-Scully noisy; the ideal sd depends on games per team.
Leagues with unbalanced schedules (teams not all playing each other equally) violate the round-robin assumption behind Noll-Scully.
Win share Gini has a floor and ceiling set by the schedule, not only by team quality.
references: Rottenberg, S. (1956). The baseball players' labor market. Journal of Political Economy, 64(3), 242-258.
Fort, R., & Quirk, J. (1995). Cross-subsidization, incentives, and outcomes in professional team sports leagues. Journal of Economic Literature, 33(3), 1265-1299.
Scully, G. W. (1989). The Business of Major League Baseball. University of Chicago Press.
Gini, C. (1912). Variabilità e mutabilità. Tipografia di Paolo Cuppini, Bologna.
Sevenhuysen, T. Oracle's Elixir: LoL esports match data. https://oracleselixir.com/tools/downloads

data.source: Oracle's Elixir professional League of Legends match data (yearly CSV files).

competitive_balance.definition: Regular-season games only (playoffs and international events excluded). Teams with fewer than 5 games in a tournament are left out; tournaments with fewer than 4 such teams are left out. Concentrated quantity: each team's share of all regular-season wins in the tournament. Noll-Scully = sd(win%) / (0.5/sqrt(mean games)).

upset_rate.definition: Share of games won by the team with the lower pre-game Elo (games with equal ratings and the Elo burn-in period excluded). Higher values mean less predictable results under Elo.

placements.definition: Regular-season rank (by game win %, ties share the better rank) of the derived champion of each split with both a regular season and playoffs in the data. Rank 6 = 6th or lower.

findings: 654 league splits analysed; median Noll-Scully ratio 1.64 (range 0.45 to 3.61).
Linear trend in the median Noll-Scully ratio by season year: -0.003 per year over 7 seasons with at least 20 splits (2020 to 2026; descriptive, not a significance test).

Median Gini of wins per split 0.258; median normalised HHI of win shares 0.0279. A round-robin limits how unequal win shares can get, so these values are small by construction; compare them across leagues and years, not with market HHI thresholds.
The best regular-season team went on to win the derived title in 52% of 408 splits.
Across 72745 games after the Elo burn-in, the lower-rated team won 36.1% of the time.
data.interpretation: Values above 1 mean results are more spread out than chance alone would produce, i.e. real differences in team strength. How far above 1 is the measure of imbalance.
